text: Work energy theorem. According to Newton's second law, the net force, all forces acting on a particle, determines the rate of change of the momentum of the particle or its motion. Therefore, we should consider the work done by all the forces acting on a particle or the net work to see what effect it has on the particle's motion. Consider the net work done on a particle that moves over an infinitesimal displacement or DW subnet equals vector f subnet dot d vector r. Newton's second law tells us that we can transform the net force vector f subnet using the acceleration d vector v over dt. So, dw subnet equals m times d vector v over dt dot d vector r. Using the definition of velocity, d vector r equals vector v times dt. We have dw subnet equals m times d vector v over dt dot vector v times dt. Equals m vector v dot d vector v over dt dt. Equals m vector v dot d vector v, where we also used the commutative property of the dot product. We can represent the dot product in terms of Cartesian coordinates and then include the result in the integral between two points a and b on the particle's trajectory. This gives us the work done on the particle as w subnet a b equals integral from a to b m v sub x d v sub x plus m v sub y d v sub y plus m v sub z d v sub z. Equals 1 half m times the quantity v sub x squared plus v sub y squared plus v sub z squared evaluated from a to b equals 1 half m v squared evaluated from a to b equals k sub b minus k sub a. We use the relation for v squared equals v sub x squared plus v sub y squared plus v sub z squared to reduce the expression and the definition of a particle's kinetic energy k. The result is called the work energy theorem. Work energy theorem. The network on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. W subnet equals k sub f minus k sub i equals 1 half m times the quantity v sub f squared minus v sub i squared. According to this theorem, when an object slows down, meaning v sub f is less than v sub i, its final kinetic energy is less than the initial kinetic energy and the network done on it is negative. Or speeds up, meaning v sub f is greater than v sub i, its final kinetic energy is greater than the initial kinetic energy and the network done on it is positive. When calculating the network, you must include all the forces acting on an object. If you leave out any forces or include extra forces not acting on the object, you will get a wrong result. The importance of the work energy theorem is that it makes some calculations much simpler to accomplish compared to solving them with Newton's second law. For example, we obtained the acceleration of a block on a frictionless incline as a equals g sine theta using Newton's second law in chapter 5, example problem, weight on an incline. If we also use the kinematic equation for acceleration, v sub f squared equals v sub i squared plus 2a times s sub f minus s sub i, then we could find that v sub f squared equals v sub i squared plus 2g times s sub f minus s sub i sine theta, where s sub f and s sub i are the initial and final positions on the incline respectively. Once Newton's second law gives the acceleration, the same result follows from the kinematics tools in chapter 3. We can also get this result from the work energy theorem in equation. Since only two forces are acting on the object, gravity and the normal force, normal force doesn't do work, the network is just the work done by gravity. The infinitesimal work, dw, is the dot product of gravity, vector f sub g equals negative mg j hat, and the infinitesimal displacement, d vector r equals dx i hat plus dy j hat. Applying the work energy theorem, we have w sub net equals the integral from y sub i to y sub f vector f sub g dot d vector r equals the integral from y sub i to y sub f minus mg dy equals minus mg integral from y sub i to y sub f dy equals minus mg y, evaluated from y sub i to y sub f equals minus mg times the quantity y sub f minus y sub i. We have found the left hand side of the work energy theorem where we now set it equal to the change in kinetic energy, minus mg times the quantity y sub f minus y sub i equals 1.5m times the quantity v sub f square. v sub f squared minus v sub i squared. In example problem, weight on an incline, the change in height y sub f minus y sub i forms the short side of a right triangle with the same angle theta from the incline. The hypotenuse of the triangle is s sub f minus s sub i along the incline. Therefore, we can show that the short side of the triangle is y sub f minus y sub i equals minus s sub f minus s sub i sine theta using our trigonometric identity for sine theta. Note s is defined to increase down the incline to the left in the figure which introduces the minus sign. We can then obtain mg times the quantity s sub f minus s sub i sine theta equals 1.5m times the quantity v sub f squared minus v sub i squared. v sub f squared equals v sub i squared plus 2g times the quantity s sub f minus s sub i sine theta. Checkmark. What is gained by using the work energy theorem? For a frictionless plane, not much. Newton's second law is easy to solve only for this particular case, whereas the work energy theorem gives the final speed for any shaped frictionless surface. For an arbitrary curved surface, the normal is not constant, where it may be difficult or impossible to solve analytically using Newton's second law. For motion along a surface, the normal force never does any work because it's perpendicular to the displacement. A calculation using the work energy theorem avoids this difficulty and applies to more general solutions. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. A cart moves around a frictionless loop at constant speed. Is the network necessarily zero? Explain using the change in kinetic energy. Problem solving strategy. Work. Energy. Theorem. First, draw a free body diagram for the object or system of interest. Include only the forces acting on that object or system. Second, identify the displacement over which the work is done. For each force, decide whether it has a component parallel or anti-parallel to the displacement. Forces perpendicular to the displacement do zero work. Third, calculate the work done by each force keeping the sign of each contribution. A force that helps the motion does positive work, while a force that opposes the motion does negative work. Fourth, add the work contributions to find the network, W subnet equals delta K equals K sub F minus K sub I. Sixth, solve for the unknown quantity such as speed, force, distance, or work. Seventh, check the result using the sign of the network. If the object moves at constant speed, then delta K equals zero, and the network must be zero. If W subnet is greater than zero, the object speeds up and its kinetic energy increases. If W subnet is less than zero, the object slows down and its kinetic energy decreases. Focus on why work is not just force times distance, but the part of the force acting along the displacement and transferring energy into or out of the object's motion. Interactive simulation, energy skatepark. Use this FET simulation to connect work, kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, and energy conservation. Start with the intro or measure screen, and compare how the skater's speed changes at high and low points on the track. Then add friction or use the graphing tools to see how mechanical energy changes when non-conservative forces do work. Example problem, loop the loop. The problem. The frictionless track for a toy car includes a loop the loop of radius R. How high measured from the bottom of the loop must the car be placed to start from rest on the approaching section of track and go all the way around the loop? The work solution follows. The model. The car is treated as a point mass moving on a frictionless track in a vertical plane. Gravity points downward and does work while the normal force from the track points perpendicular to the motion and does no work. No work. The car starts from rest at height Y sub 1 above the bottom of the loop and must maintain contact at the top of the loop. At the top, the required centripetal acceleration points downward toward the center of the circle. The math. For motion from the starting point to the top of the loop, the work energy theorem relates the work done by gravity to the kinetic energy at the top. The top of the loop is at height Y sub 2 equals 2R. Minus MG times Y sub 2 minus Y sub 1 equals 1 half MV sub 2 squared. At the top of the loop, the forces acting on the car are gravity downward and the normal force downward toward the center of the loop. Newton's second law in the radial direction gives the centripetal force condition. MV sub 2 squared over R equals N plus MG. The minimum starting height occurs when the car just maintains contact with the track, so the limiting normal force is N equals 0. The required speed at the top follows from this limiting centripetal force condition. MV sub 2 squared over R equals MG. V sub 2 squared equals GR. The starting height follows by substituting the minimum top speed into the work energy equation and solving for Y sub 1. Minus MG times 2R minus Y sub 1 equals 1 half MGR. 2R minus Y sub 1 equals minus R over 2. Y sub 1 equals 5R over 2. The conclusion. The car must start from a minimum height of Y sub 1 equals 5R over 2 above the bottom of the loop. This height gives the car just enough speed at the top for gravity alone to provide the required centripetal acceleration with the normal force reduced to 0 at the limiting case. The result shows how the work energy theorem determines the speed at a critical point, while Newton's second law supplies the contact condition needed to complete the loop. Example problem. Determining a stopping force. The problem. A bullet has a mass of 40 grains, 2.6 grams, and a muzzle velocity of 1100 feet per second, 335 meters per second. It can penetrate 8 1-inch pine boards, each with thickness 0.75 inches. What is the average stopping force exerted by the wood? The worked solution follows. The model. The bullet is treated as a point mass moving in a straight line through the boards. The wood exerts an average stopping force opposite the bullet's motion over the full penetration distance. Gravity and air resistance are neglected because the stopping interaction is dominated by the wood over a short distance. The bullet comes to rest, so the wood removes the bullet's initial kinetic energy. The math. The total stopping distance is the combined thickness of the 8 boards. Delta S equals 8 times 0.75 inches, equals 6 inches, equals 0.152 meters. The stopping force points opposite the motion, so its work is negative. The work energy theorem relates the work to the loss of the bullet's initial kinetic energy. Minus F sub-av delta S equals minus K sub-i. The average stopping force follows by solving the work energy equation for the force magnitude. F sub-av equals K sub-i over delta S equals 1-half MV squared over delta S. The numerical value follows by evaluating the force expression using the given mass, speed, and stopping distance. F sub-av equals 1-half times the quantity 2.6 times 10 to the negative 3 kilograms times 335 meters per second squared over 0.152 meters, equals 960 nuutens. The conclusion. The average stopping force exerted by the wood on the bullet is 960 nuutens. This force is the constant force equivalent that would remove the bullet's initial kinetic energy over the total penetration distance. The result connects force, distance, and kinetic energy through the work energy theorem, and shows why short stopping distances can produce large forces.
